subtype: Approach: taking a holiday and returning to the same conditions [Pitfall]
passage: When Taniya came back from her week in Goa, she looked ten years younger: sun on her face, laughing, telling the whole floor about a sunrise swim. I sat two desks away and was glad for her. On Monday the same inbox was waiting, three meetings back to back, and a deadline that had crept forward while she was away. By the second week she was answering emails at ten at night again. By the fourth she had stopped laughing at lunch, was snapping at small things, and sometimes stared at the ceiling in the middle of meetings. I don't know what was going on in her head. I do know nothing at work had changed while she was away, and the holiday's glow faded fast. - Thomas

qa.q: Where did Taniya spend her week away?
What might Taniya have been feeling by the fourth week?
qa.a: Thomas can only guess, but Taniya seemed strained and irritable, snapping at small things and staring at the ceiling in meetings.

qa.q: What could Taniya do differently after the next break?
qa.a: Taniya could ask the manager to change the workload and meeting load before or on return, and see a doctor if the tiredness comes back.

qa.q: How does Thomas explain why the holiday did not last?
qa.a: Thomas sees that nothing at work changed while Taniya was away, so the same pressure was waiting.

grounding: Taniya returns refreshed from a week away to the same workload and meetings, and the exhaustion returns within a month.

subtype: Approach: taking a holiday and returning to the same conditions [Pitfall]
passage:
Saturday, 5 October. Vidya sits on a beach-shack bench in Goa, feet in the sand, phone switched off for the first time in a year. She sleeps nine hours and texts her brother, Bhupen: "I feel human again 😊"
Monday, 14 October. Back at the agency: forty-two unread emails, the same four client calls a day, the same Thursday pitch meeting that runs till eight. Nothing has changed while she was away. She tells herself the holiday charged her battery.
Tuesday, 12 November. Bhupen calls. Vidya admits she is awake at 3 am again, snapping at the junior designer and dreading Mondays. "But I just had a holiday," she says, puzzled and a little angry with herself.
Bhupen asks gently, "Did anything at work change?"
She is quiet for a long time.

qa.q: How many unread emails were waiting for Vidya on 14 October?
How does Vidya feel when the old signs return despite the holiday?
qa.a: She is puzzled and a little angry with herself, as if the holiday should have been enough.

qa.q: What could Vidya change now, beyond booking another holiday?
qa.a: She could look at the client calls and the long Thursday meetings and talk with her manager about changing them, since those causes were untouched.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see what is happening to his sister?
qa.a: Bhupen can see from outside that she came back to the same conditions, so his gentle question points her toward the real causes.

grounding: It shows a woman refreshed by a week in Goa returning to the same workload and meetings, so within a month the exhaustion is back because nothing changed.

subtype: Approach: taking a holiday and returning to the same conditions [Pitfall]
passage:
Jyoti leaned on the counter of the Aizawl branch and told the new trainee: "Let me tell you about Lalremsiami. When she was about your age, maybe twenty-five, she was the best clerk here and the most tired. She worked most Saturdays too. One March she took a whole week in Goa. She came back sunburnt and laughing, with cashew sweets for everyone. I thought, good, she's fixed.
But nothing here had changed. Same double counter, same Saturday shifts, same manager piling on reports. Within about three weeks she was quiet again. By April she was forgetting lunch and rubbing her eyes at four o'clock. She said to me once, 'The holiday was lovely. But I came back to the same chair.'
That line stayed with me. The next year, when I became manager, I stopped the Saturday shifts."

qa.q: Where did Lalremsiami go for a week?
qa.a: She took a whole week in Goa.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when she said she came back to the same chair?
qa.a: She felt weary and a bit defeated, seeing that a lovely holiday could not undo conditions that were still the same.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have kept the holiday's benefit, and why?
qa.a: Changing the Saturday shifts or the report load when she returned, because the holiday only rested her while the causes stayed in place.

qa.q: How did Jyoti see Lalremsiami's return, first and later?
qa.a: At first Jyoti thought she was fixed, but watching her go quiet again made Jyoti see that the job itself needed changing.

grounding: It shows a young clerk refreshed by a week in Goa going back to the same shifts and reports, so the exhaustion returns within weeks because the causes were unchanged.
